books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925

stimulus.text:
President Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925 (verbatim excerpt):

"After all, the chief business of the American people is business. They are profoundly concerned with producing, buying, selling, investing and prospering in the world. I am strongly of opinion that the great majority of people will always find these are moving impulses of our life."

"We make no concealment of the fact that we want wealth, but there are many other things that we want very much more. We want peace and honor, and that charity which is so strong an element of all civilization. The chief ideal of the American people is idealism."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925, public domain (American Presidency Project).

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Calvin Coolidge, Address to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, January 17, 1925
stem: Coolidge's address best reflects which attitude of the 1920s?

options.text: Wealth was the chief end of existence
options.misconception: Coolidge says wealth is not the chief end of existence. The speech limits the praise of wealth, not just celebrates it.

options.text: Government should run the largest companies directly
options.misconception: Coolidge wanted business to lead, with government in the background. He never asks the government to run companies.

options.text: Business served ideals larger than mere profit
Americans cared about nothing except making money
options.misconception: The speech says Americans want wealth and also many other things. Caring about money is not the same as caring only about money.

rationales.A: Coolidge says wealth is not the chief end of existence. The speech limits the praise of wealth, not just celebrates it.
rationales.B: Coolidge wanted business to lead, with government in the background. He never asks the government to run companies.
rationales.C: Coolidge praises business, then says wealth is only a means, and that peace, honor, and charity matter more. Business serves ideals larger than profit.
rationales.D: The speech says Americans want wealth and also many other things. Caring about money is not the same as caring only about money.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first paragraph: business is the chief business of Americans.
2. Read the second: wealth is a means, and peace, honor, and charity matter more.
3. Put them together: Coolidge praises business and still sets moral limits on it.
4. Check the common misreading: the famous short version drops the limits, but the speech keeps them.
Remember: read the whole passage before judging it, since the second half can limit the first.
